title: Shelters
about: Staying warm and dry for a night: debris huts, tarp shelters, and insulating from the ground.

articles.title: Build a debris hut
articles.intro: A tight, leaf-filled shelter that keeps you warm without a fire.
steps: Find a ridge pole a little longer than you are tall. Rest one end on a stump or a fork about waist high.
Lean sticks along both sides of the pole, close together, to make a ribcage.
Pile leaves, grass and pine needles over it, at least an arm's length thick.
Fill the inside with dry leaves too, and block the doorway with a pile of leaves once inside.
Keep it just big enough to lie in: small shelters stay warmer.
avoid: Don't build in a dip where cold air and water collect, or under dead branches.

articles.title: Tarp shelter
articles.intro: A tarp, poncho or survival blanket makes a quick rain-proof roof.
steps: Tie a ridge line between two trees at chest height (clove hitch at one end, taut-line hitch at the other).
Hang the tarp over it and stake or weigh down the edges, low on the windward side.
Angle it so rain runs off and doesn't pool.
Lie on insulation, not on the bare ground.
avoid: Don't pitch it facing into the wind.

articles.title: Stay off the cold ground
articles.intro: The ground pulls heat out of you far faster than air. Insulation underneath matters more than a roof.
steps: Gather a bed of dry leaves, grass, pine boughs or your pack, at least 15 cm thick when squashed.
Lie on it, not on bare earth or rock.
Add more under hips and shoulders, where you press down most.
Wet? Even a layer of branches keeps you out of the water.
avoid: Don't sleep directly on snow, rock or wet soil.
